screens.title: Load-Use Hazards and Pipeline Stalls
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will explore the load-use hazard, the single most persistent data hazard in a simple in-order pipeline with forwarding. You will learn why forwarding cannot resolve this class of RAW hazard, how the hazard detection unit implements a one-cycle stall that freezes IF and ID and inserts a bubble into EX, and how that stall changes CPI. We will step through the five-stage timing that makes the mismatch inevitable, calculate the CPI cost with a concrete numeric example, and then study software and hardware strategies that reduce stalls. The compiler-side approach uses instruction scheduling and loop unrolling to move independent work into the delay slot. Hardware-side solutions include speculative load execution, load buffering, and value prediction. Finally, we will frame the practical trade-offs: when to rely on compiler scheduling and when hardware complexity is justified. By the end you should be able to detect load-use pairs, implement the simple stall logic, and reason about whether a software or hardware approach is the right fit for a given workload.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Load-Use Hazards
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Load-Use Hazards and Pipeline Stalls

Understand the timing mismatch that forces a stall, see how the hardware detects it, and learn compiler patterns that avoid the penalty.

Why it matters
In-order pipelines often pay these stalls frequently in pointer-heavy code.
Orientation

You will step through the five-stage timing, implement the simple stall reaction, compute CPI impact using the formula CPI = CPI_base + p × 1, and practice scheduling to hide delays. Examples focus on load followed immediately by a dependent arithmetic instruction.

What you'll practice
  • Detecting load-use pairs
  • Inserting a pipeline bubble
  • Scheduling instructions to avoid stalls
Explore Key Topics
Load-Use Timing
Why the data from MEM is available too late for an immediate dependent EX stage.
Stall Mechanics
Freezing IF/ID and inserting a NOP into EX to allow forwarding from MEM/WB.
Scheduling & Unrolling
How compilers move independent instructions between load and use to hide the one-cycle delay.
Concept Snapshot
Data ready at end of MEM, dependent needs it at start of EX — timing mismatch.
Stall: freeze IF/ID, insert bubble into EX, forward from MEM/WB in the next cycle.
Quick Example
LW R1, 0(R2)
ADD R3, R1, R4  # dependent: causes 1-cycle stall if scheduled immediately
Compiler can insert an independent instruction between the load and add to avoid the stall.

You will also recognize pointer-chasing code patterns that make p large and understand when hardware techniques such as speculative loads or value prediction might be needed. Each objective ties a practical skill to why it matters: detecting hazards prevents incorrect execution, implementing stalls preserves correctness at low hardware cost, calculating CPI quantifies impact, and scheduling reduces stalls without extra hardware complexity. screens.title: What is a load-use hazard?
screens.narratorSegment: A load-use hazard occurs when an instruction uses a register value that was loaded by the immediately preceding load instruction. The key timing claim is simple: the load's data becomes available at the end of its memory stage, while the dependent instruction needs that same data at the start of its execute stage. In a standard five-stage pipeline this mismatch means forwarding paths cannot supply the value in time if the dependent instruction follows the load without delay. Concretely, if you have LW R1, 0(R2) followed immediately by ADD R3, R1, R4, the ADD will reach its EX stage before the load's data is ready to be forwarded, so executing without a stall would use a stale or incorrect value. A common misconception is that forwarding handles all RAW hazards; forwarding fixes many cases but cannot change when the load's data physically arrives. The practical consequence is that we must either insert a one-cycle stall or schedule independent instructions into the gap. As you learn this material, remember that the load-use hazard is about timing — not correctness of the instruction semantics — and the stall preserves correct program behavior. How would you spot this pattern in an instruction stream?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A load-use hazard happens when a dependent instruction needs load data before it is available; forwarding can't bridge the end-of-MEM to start-of-EX timing gap.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › What is a load-use hazard?
Definition

A load-use hazard occurs when an instruction uses a register loaded by the immediately preceding load, and the loaded value is not available in time for the dependent instruction's execute stage.

Concrete example
LW R1, 0(R2)
ADD R3, R1, R4  # dependent: requires R1 at start of EX
Why it matters
Without a stall or scheduling, the dependent instruction would execute with incorrect timing and produce wrong results or require complex replaying logic.
Common misconception
Forwarding resolves all RAW hazards. In fact, forwarding cannot supply a load's data early enough because the data is only ready at the end of memory access.
Quick diagnostic checklist
  • Is the previous instruction a load? (MEM read)
  • Does the next instruction read the same register as source? (use in EX)
  • Is there any independent instruction between them? If not, a stall is needed.
Key takeaway
The load-use hazard is a timing problem; the correct fix is either a controlled stall or instruction reordering that preserves semantics while creating time for the load.

screens.title: Five-stage timing that creates the mismatch
screens.narratorSegment: Let's step through the five-stage pipeline cycles to see exactly when the load's data is produced and why the dependent instruction misses it. Assume a load instruction moves through IF, ID, EX, MEM, and WB across consecutive cycles. The data read from memory becomes available at the end of the MEM stage, and the register file write happens during WB. A dependent instruction that follows immediately will be in EX one cycle earlier — it needs the register operand at the beginning of its EX stage. Walking the cycles shows the mismatch: when LW is in MEM at cycle four, its dependent has already completed EX at cycle three and therefore cannot receive the loaded data in time. A one-cycle stall forces the dependent instruction to delay its EX stage until the load's data is available in the MEM/WB boundary so forwarding can supply it. A common misreading is to think writeback timing alone is the issue; the critical point is that forwarding can only forward data when it is present, and the load's data simply arrives too late for an immediately following EX. Given this timing, the simplest correct hardware response is a one-cycle stall that inserts a bubble into EX, letting MEM complete and data be forwarded to the delayed instruction.

keyIdea.title: Timing walkthrough
keyIdea.text: Data from the load is available at the end of MEM; the dependent needs it at the start of EX — a one-cycle delay fixes the mismatch so forwarding can work.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Five-stage timing
Cycle-by-cycle example
LW and ADD progression over cycles (abstract):
Cycle 1: LW in IF | ADD in IF
Cycle 2: LW in ID | ADD in ID
Cycle 3: LW in EX | ADD in EX  <- ADD needs R1 now
Cycle 4: LW in MEM (data ready at end of cycle)
Cycle 5: LW in WB  | ADD can use forwarded data in EX
Note that ADD's EX stage occurs before the load's MEM stage completes, causing the inability to forward in time. The stall inserts one cycle so ADD's EX happens when data is available.
Implication
  • Data from LW is not ready during the EX of the following instruction.
  • Forwarding cannot create data earlier than MEM produces it.
  • One-cycle stall aligns the dependent EX with the load's MEM/WB availability.
Concrete correction
Stall IF/ID for one cycle, insert bubble into EX, then allow MEM and WB to proceed; the dependent executes EX when the data is available and can be forwarded.

screens.title: Why forwarding cannot resolve load-use
screens.narratorSegment: Forwarding is excellent at resolving many read-after-write hazards because it takes a value as soon as it exists in later pipeline stages and supplies it to an earlier dependent stage. However, forwarding cannot conjure data before it has been produced. With a load instruction the data is only produced when the memory read completes, at the end of the MEM stage. If the dependent instruction's EX stage happens earlier, there is simply no value in a later stage to forward. Contrast this with a case where the previous instruction is an ALU operation: the result is available at the end of EX and can be forwarded into the next EX stage in time. A common misconception is to equate all RAW hazards with a forwarding solution; this is incorrect because the source of data matters. In short, a register written by an ALU instruction can be forwarded because the result exists earlier; a register written by a load does not. This timing contrast is the precise reason load-use hazards require special treatment — either a stall or rearrangement of instructions to delay the use.

keyIdea.title: Forwarding limitation
keyIdea.text: Forwarding resolves ALU-to-use RAW hazards but cannot help when the value is only produced after memory read completes; timing is the difference.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Forwarding vs Load
ALU result (forwardable)
When an ALU instruction produces a result in EX, that result can be forwarded immediately into the next instruction's EX stage. This supplies the dependent exactly when needed without extra cycles.
Example: 
ADD R1, R2, R3
SUB R4, R1, R5  # forwarded from ALU result
Load result (not early enough)
A load produces its value at the end of MEM. If the dependent instruction is immediately next, its EX happens before MEM finishes, so there is nothing to forward in time.
Example: 
LW R1, 0(R2)
ADD R3, R1, R4  # needs R1 too early -> stall required
Takeaway
Forwarding depends on when data is produced. If production occurs later than the dependent's demand, use scheduling or stalls to align timing.

screens.title: Stall implementation mechanics
screens.narratorSegment: When hazard detection logic recognizes a load-use pattern it executes a small, precise sequence of control actions to preserve correct execution: first, it stalls the IF and ID stages so the program counter does not advance and the instruction in ID is held in place. Second, it inserts a bubble — effectively a NOP — into the EX stage by preventing ID/EX from being updated; this bubble gives the load one cycle to move from EX into MEM so its data will be ready. The MEM and WB stages are allowed to proceed normally. The result is that the dependent instruction remains in ID for one extra cycle, then proceeds into EX when the data can be forwarded from MEM/WB. A pitfall when implementing stalls is forgetting to freeze the PC and IF stage, which would cause instruction fetch to continue and corrupt instruction ordering. Another subtle point is to ensure control signals to EX are neutralized for the inserted bubble. Correctly implemented, the stall is a single-cycle pause that preserves semantics while keeping hardware complexity low. Stall implementation mechanics means on detection: freeze if/id and pc, insert a nop into ex, and let mem/wb proceed so forwarding supplies the load's value on the next cycle.. In practical terms, exactly what the hazard unit does on detection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Stall actions
keyIdea.text: On detection: freeze IF/ID and PC, insert a NOP into EX, and let MEM/WB proceed so forwarding supplies the load's value on the next cycle.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Stall mechanics
Stall sequence
  1. Detect ID/EX.MemRead and register overlap with IF/ID sources.
  2. Freeze IF and ID stages: PC does not increment; hold IF/ID register.
  3. Insert a bubble into EX by preventing ID/EX update (NOP signals into EX).
  4. Allow MEM and WB to continue normally so load reaches MEM and provides data.
This preserves program order and correctness with minimal extra hardware: a stall control signal and bubble insertion logic.
Common pitfalls
  • Not freezing PC/IF causes fetch to continue and misalign instruction order.
  • Failing to neutralize EX control signals for the bubble causes unintended behavior.
Key Takeaway
A one-cycle stall is a small set of control changes that preserve correctness by aligning the dependent instruction with the load's data availability.

screens.title: Hazard detection logic
screens.narratorSegment: The hazard detection condition is concise and maps directly to pipeline registers. In practice we test whether the instruction in ID/EX is a load (MemRead set) and whether its destination register equals either source register of the instruction in IF/ID. Formally: ID/EX. MemRead AND (ID/EX. Rd == IF/ID. Rs1 OR ID/EX. Rd == IF/ID. Rs2). When this condition is true the hardware must stall. This check must use the proper pipeline-stage register fields and carefully compare register numbers, including zero checks if the ISA uses a zero register. A common mistake is to compare the wrong pipeline registers or to check for MemWrite instead of MemRead. Another subtlety is ensuring the comparison happens early enough in the cycle so stall control can freeze IF and ID before they update. The detection logic is intentionally simple: it prevents incorrect data use with a single boolean and small control path, which is why it is widely used in textbook five-stage pipelines. Hazard detection logic means trigger a stall when the id/ex stage is a load and its destination matches a source of the following instruction: id/ex.memread and (id/ex.rd == if/id.rs1 or id/ex.rd == if/id.rs2).. In practical terms, the boolean condition that triggers a load-use stall. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Detection condition
keyIdea.text: Trigger a stall when the ID/EX stage is a load and its destination matches a source of the following instruction: ID/EX.MemRead AND (ID/EX.Rd == IF/ID.Rs1 OR ID/EX.Rd == IF/ID.Rs2).

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Hazard detection
Detection logic
The canonical boolean condition is shown below. It checks that the instruction in ID/EX is performing a memory read and that its destination register matches one of the sources in IF/ID.
ID/EX.MemRead && (ID/EX.Rd == IF/ID.Rs1 || ID/EX.Rd == IF/ID.Rs2)
Why MemRead?
Only loads require waiting for memory; other instructions produce data earlier and are handled by forwarding.
Register equality
Compare register IDs, taking care with encoding for register zero if the ISA defines it specially.
Misconception check
Do not check IF/ID destination registers; the comparison must use ID/EX destination against IF/ID sources to detect an imminent load-use pair.

screens.title: CPI impact and a numeric example
screens.narratorSegment: We can quantify the performance effect of one-cycle load-use stalls with a simple formula: CPI equals the base CPI plus p times one extra cycle, where p is the frequency of load-use events. That is: CPI = CPI_base + p × 1. The chapter provides a numeric example to make this concrete. If 20% of instructions are loads and half of those loads are immediately followed by a dependent use, then p = 0.20 × 0.50 = 0.10. If CPI_base is 1.0, the new CPI becomes 1.10 — a measurable 10% slowdown. In pointer-chasing workloads nearly every load is followed by a use, so p approaches the load frequency and the CPI hit can be large. A common mistake is to apply the formula using the fraction of loads alone; instead, p must reflect the fraction of all instructions that are load-use pairs. Understanding this calculation helps you decide whether to optimize with compiler scheduling, loop unrolling, or to accept hardware complexity for out-of-order execution. As you profile a program, estimate load frequency and dependent rate to compute p and the expected CPI increase.

keyIdea.title: CPI formula
keyIdea.text: CPI = CPI_base + p × 1, where p is the probability an instruction causes a load-use stall; compute p as load frequency × fraction of loads followed by a dependent.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › CPI impact
Formula
CPI = CPI_base + p × 1
Compute p as the fraction of all instructions that cause a load-use stall. For the provided example:
Given
Load frequency = 0.20, fraction of loads followed by dependent = 0.50
Compute p
p = 0.20 × 0.50 = 0.10 → CPI increases by 0.10
Example result
If CPI_base = 1.0 then CPI = 1.0 + 0.10 = 1.10, a 10% slowdown due to load-use stalls.

screens.title: Pointer-chasing and high load-use frequency
screens.narratorSegment: Pointer-chasing code — such as linked-list traversal or some tree traversals — often causes a very high rate of load-use pairs because each step loads a pointer and the next instruction immediately uses that pointer to compute the next address. In such code, almost every load is followed by a use, so the probability p approaches the load frequency itself. For example, if 25% of instructions are loads and almost every load is immediately used to compute the next memory address, p will be close to 0.25, producing a sizable CPI increase. The reason this pattern is harmful is that there are few independent instructions available to schedule into the delay slot; the program's data dependence chain prevents reordering without changing correctness. A common mistaken hope is that simple compiler scheduling will always eliminate stalls; pointer-chasing shows the limitation because there are no independent instructions to move. In these cases, hardware techniques such as out-of-order execution, load buffering, or value prediction are often necessary to regain performance. When analyzing applications, identify pointer-heavy kernels and measure p to decide whether software or hardware investment is warranted.

narration.text: Pointer-chasing code — such as linked-list traversal or some tree traversals — often causes a very high rate of load-use pairs because each step loads a pointer and the next instruction immediately uses that pointer to compute the next address. In such code, almost every load is followed by a use, so the probability p approaches the load frequency itself. For example, if 25% of instructions are loads and almost every load is immediately used to compute the next memory address, p will be close to 0.25, producing a sizable CPI increase. The reason this pattern is harmful is that there are few independent instructions available to schedule into the delay slot; the program's data dependence chain prevents reordering without changing correctness. A common mistaken hope is that simple compiler scheduling will always eliminate stalls; pointer-chasing shows the limitation because there are no independent instructions to move. In these cases, hardware techniques such as out-of-order execution, load buffering, or value prediction are often necessary to regain performance. When analyzing applications, identify pointer-heavy kernels and measure p to decide whether software or hardware investment is warranted.

keyIdea.title: Pointer-chasing effect
keyIdea.text: Pointer-chasing yields high p because loads are immediately used to compute next addresses, leaving no independent instructions to fill delay slots.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Pointer-chasing
Why pointer-chasing hurts
In pointer-chasing code each load often produces the address used by the next memory operation or compute step. That creates a chain of true data dependencies with few or no independent instructions to reorder.
Typical pattern
LOAD addr -> pointer
use pointer to compute next addr
LOAD next_addr
Result
p approaches load frequency; CPI increases significantly and compiler scheduling is often ineffective without unrolling.
Practical note
When analyzing performance, profile specific kernels for load-use frequency rather than assuming an average instruction mix.

screens.title: Compiler instruction scheduling
screens.narratorSegment: Compiler scheduling, also known as code motion or pipeline scheduling, reorders instructions so that independent operations occur between a load and its use. The goal is to fill the one-cycle delay slot and avoid the hardware stall. For example, consider three instructions: a load, an add that uses the load, and a later independent subtract. A simple scheduler can move the subtract between the load and the add, yielding no stall because the add's EX is delayed until the data arrives. A concrete before-and-after illustration: before scheduling: LW R1, 0(R2); ADD R3, R1, R4; SUB R5, R6, R7. After scheduling: LW R1, 0(R2); SUB R5, R6, R7; ADD R3, R1, R4. This transformation preserves program semantics when the moved instruction is truly independent. A common compiler pitfall is moving an instruction with hidden dependencies, such as a memory write that depends on computed addresses. The compiler must verify independence conservatively. Also, scheduling opportunities depend on available independent instructions; if none exist the compiler cannot eliminate the stall without unrolling or changing algorithms. Practice writing a simple pass that scans blocks, locates load-use pairs, and searches for movable instructions to fill the delay slot.

keyIdea.text: Reorder independent instructions between a load and its use to eliminate the one-cycle stall, preserving correctness only when independence is verified.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Compiler scheduling
Before scheduling
LW R1, 0(R2)    # Load
ADD R3, R1, R4  # Use (causes 1-cycle stall)
SUB R5, R6, R7  # Independent
After scheduling
LW R1, 0(R2)    # Load
SUB R5, R6, R7  # Independent moved into delay slot
ADD R3, R1, R4  # Use (no stall)
Compiler checks
The compiler must prove the moved instruction has no data or memory dependence on the load or its use. Conservative analysis may limit opportunities, especially with memory aliasing.

screens.title: Scheduling practice: sequences A, B, C
screens.narratorSegment: Now let's apply a scheduling pass to three example sequences to see how many load-use stalls can be eliminated. Sequence A is LW, ADD dependent on the load, then an independent SUB and an independent AND. The scheduler can place one of those independent instructions between the load and ADD, removing the single one-cycle stall. Sequence B has LW, ADD dependent on the load, then SUB that reads the load destination—this SUB depends on the same load, so it cannot be moved; the scheduler cannot eliminate the stall. Sequence C is a loop body with two loads and two dependent adds; with care the scheduler may interleave instructions if the loads are independent, but often there are limits. The hands-on activity described in the chapter asks you to write a pass that searches for load-use pairs, looks ahead for movable instructions, and reorders them. When no instruction can be moved, the pass should insert a NOP or leave the stall. This exercise highlights the limitations of scheduling: without independent instructions available you cannot remove the stall without unrolling or changing algorithms.

keyIdea.title: Practice schedule
keyIdea.text: Sequence A: stall eliminated; Sequence B: stall unavoidable; Sequence C: depends on independence of loads and potential for reordering or unrolling.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Scheduling practice
Sequence A
LW R1, 0(R2)
ADD R3, R1, R4
SUB R5, R6, R7
AND R8, R9, R10
Scheduler can move SUB or AND between LW and ADD to eliminate the stall.
Sequence B
LW R1, 0(R2)
ADD R3, R1, R4
SUB R5, R1, R6
SUB depends on R1 as well, so it cannot be moved to fill the delay slot. Stall is unavoidable without unrolling.
Sequence C (loop)
LW R1, 0(R2)
ADD R3, R1, R4
LW R5, 0(R6)
ADD R7, R5, R8
Scheduling may rearrange between independent loads, but if dependencies form chains, unrolling can create room for scheduling; otherwise stalls remain.
Activity
Write a pass that finds load-use pairs, searches forward for independent instructions, and moves one into the delay slot; if none found, insert a NOP or leave the stall.

screens.title: Loop unrolling to create scheduling opportunities
screens.narratorSegment: Loop unrolling duplicates the loop body multiple times to produce more independent instructions inside the expanded body. This creates additional candidates that the scheduler can move into delay slots between a load and its use. For example, a loop whose body is a single load and dependent add offers no scheduling room. After unrolling twice the body contains two loads and two adds; the compiler can then interleave load2 and add1 to hide the delay. The benefit is reduced stalls and lower branch overhead, often improving CPI substantially. The trade-offs are increased code size and higher register pressure, which may spill and offset the gains. Also, aggressive unrolling may expose additional opportunities for instruction-level parallelism, but requires careful register allocation and sometimes profile-guided heuristics. A common misconception is that unrolling always helps; in register-limited code the added pressure can make performance worse. Use unrolling selectively on hot loops where profiling shows high p and available registers to hold temporaries. Loop unrolling to create scheduling opportunities means unrolling increases instruction density and independent work, giving the scheduler more choices to fill load-use delay slots; but it costs code size and may increase register pressure.. In practical terms, how unrolling helps and its trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Loop unrolling
How unrolling creates room
Original loop body with no scheduling room:
LW R1, 0(R2)
ADD R3, R1, R4
After unrolling twice, the body has more instructions the compiler can interleave:
LW R1, 0(R2)
ADD R3, R1, R4
LW R5, 0(R6)
ADD R7, R5, R8
Scheduler can reorder to place independent instructions between loads and uses, removing some stalls. Evaluate register pressure and code size before applying aggressively.
Trade-offs
Unrolling increases code size and may raise register pressure, which can introduce spills that hurt performance; use profiling to guide unrolling.

screens.title: Hardware approaches: speculative loads, buffering, and value prediction
screens.narratorSegment: When compiler techniques cannot remove load-use stalls because dependencies are inherent, hardware can help. Speculative load execution in out-of-order processors allows loads to be issued earlier than program order, overlapping memory access with other work and often reducing the perceived delay. Load buffering lets the processor make load data available from a buffer before it is written back to the register file, enabling dependent instructions to read from the buffer when safe. Value prediction attempts to guess the loaded value and execute dependent instructions speculatively; if the prediction is correct the stall is avoided, but on misprediction the dependent must be replayed. Each technique reduces stalls at increasing hardware complexity and risk. A common misconception is that hardware always beats software; in many cases a combined approach is best. For pointer-chasing or deep dependent chains hardware methods can provide material benefits, but they add verification, complexity, and potential replays that must be managed carefully. Hardware approaches: speculative loads, buffering, and value prediction means speculative load execution, load buffering, and value prediction can hide or eliminate load-use stalls when compiler scheduling cannot, at the cost of extra hardware complexity and recovery logic.. In practical terms, when software scheduling is insufficient. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Hardware techniques
Speculative loads
Issue loads earlier out-of-order so their memory accesses overlap other work. Reduces observed latency but requires mechanisms to check memory ordering correctness.
Load buffering
Buffer load data allowing dependent instructions to read from the buffer before the value is written back to the register file, enabling earlier use.
Value prediction
Predict the load's value and execute dependent instructions speculatively. On misprediction, replay the dependent instructions, which costs cycles.
Practical trade-offs
Hardware removes some software limits but increases complexity and verification cost. Use profiling to justify hardware investment for critical workloads like pointer-chasing.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Summarizing the essentials: load-use hazards arise because loads produce data at the end of MEM while uses need it at the start of EX, creating a timing gap forwarding cannot bridge. The hardware fix is a one-cycle stall that freezes IF/ID and inserts a bubble into EX; the detection logic is ID/EX. MemRead AND register equality to IF/ID sources. The CPI impact is measured by CPI = CPI_base + p × 1, where p is the frequency of load-use pairs. Compiler scheduling and loop unrolling are effective software strategies when independent instructions are available; when they are not, hardware techniques like speculative loads, load buffering, or value prediction may be required. Pointer-chasing code often pushes p high and limits compiler options. Keep these compact rules in mind when optimizing: detect load-use patterns, quantify p, try scheduling and selective unrolling, and only add hardware complexity when software cannot solve the problem.

Load-use timing
Data ready at end of MEM, needed at start of EX.
Stall mechanism
Freeze IF/ID and insert bubble into EX to wait for data.
Detection logic
ID/EX.MemRead AND (ID/EX.Rd == IF/ID.Rs1 OR ID/EX.Rd == IF/ID.Rs2).

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three concise rules in mind. First, recognize the load-use timing gap: the load's value arrives at end of MEM while the dependent wants it at start of EX. Second, use the simple hardware response: detect the pattern, stall IF/ID, and insert a bubble into EX so forwarding can supply the value in the following cycle. Third, prefer compiler scheduling and loop unrolling when independent instructions exist; otherwise consider hardware approaches like speculative loads, load buffering, or value prediction. These three rules will let you analyze a workload, compute the CPI cost using p, and choose an appropriate mitigation strategy based on available code structure and acceptable hardware complexity. What to Remember means 1) timing gap matters. 2) stall correctly to preserve correctness. 3) use scheduling first, hardware only when necessary.. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › What to Remember
Timing gap
Data is ready at end of MEM but needed at start of EX.
Stall action
Freeze IF/ID, insert bubble in EX, forward from MEM/WB next cycle.
Mitigation
Try scheduling and unrolling first; use hardware techniques only when dependencies prevent software fixes.
Final reflective question: for a hot loop with p measured at 0.20 and limited independent instructions, would you first hand-tune code, unroll, or advocate hardware features? The answer depends on cost, code-size budget, and whether the workload is stable across deployments.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will explore the load-use hazard, the single most persistent data hazard in a simple in-order pipeline with forwarding. You will learn why forwarding cannot resolve this class of RAW hazard, how the hazard detection unit implements a one-cycle stall that freezes IF and ID and inserts a bubble into EX, and how that stall changes CPI. We will step through the five-stage timing that makes the mismatch inevitable, calculate the CPI cost with a concrete numeric example, and then study software and hardware strategies that reduce stalls. The compiler-side approach uses instruction scheduling and loop unrolling to move independent work into the delay slot. Hardware-side solutions include speculative load execution, load buffering, and value prediction. Finally, we will frame the practical trade-offs: when to rely on compiler scheduling and when hardware complexity is justified. By the end you should be able to detect load-use pairs, implement the simple stall logic, and reason about whether a software or hardware approach is the right fit for a given workload.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why the load-use hazard is the single data hazard that forwarding cannot eliminate, implement the simple hardware stall that resolves the timing mismatch, compute the performance cost using the CPI = CPI_base + p × 1 formula, and apply compiler scheduling and loop unrolling to reduce stalls. You will also recognize pointer-chasing code patterns that make p large and understand when hardware techniques such as speculative loads or value prediction might be needed. Each objective ties a practical skill to why it matters: detecting hazards prevents incorrect execution, implementing stalls preserves correctness at low hardware cost, calculating CPI quantifies impact, and scheduling reduces stalls without extra hardware complexity. These competencies prepare you to reason about trade-offs between software and hardware solutions in system design.

This second objectives slide focuses on diagnosis and advanced mitigation. You will learn to identify pointer-chasing and other patterns that make the load-use frequency p large, and measure how much CPI increases using sampled instruction mixes. You will practice reading the hazard detection condition and mapping it to pipeline registers. Finally, you'll weigh hardware options such as speculative loads and value prediction against compiler approaches like unrolling. These advanced objectives ensure you can both reason quantitatively about performance and choose an appropriate solution: software scheduling when code allows, or hardware mechanisms when dependencies are inherent. A practical outcome is being able to explain, with numbers, whether a given workload benefits from compiler reordering or from adding hardware complexity. Learning Objectives (continued) means diagnose high p workloads, read hazard detection logic, and compare compiler vs. hardware mitigations using quantitative reasoning.. In practical terms, deeper skills and diagnostics. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A load-use hazard occurs when an instruction uses a register value that was loaded by the immediately preceding load instruction. The key timing claim is simple: the load's data becomes available at the end of its memory stage, while the dependent instruction needs that same data at the start of its execute stage. In a standard five-stage pipeline this mismatch means forwarding paths cannot supply the value in time if the dependent instruction follows the load without delay. Concretely, if you have LW R1, 0(R2) followed immediately by ADD R3, R1, R4, the ADD will reach its EX stage before the load's data is ready to be forwarded, so executing without a stall would use a stale or incorrect value. A common misconception is that forwarding handles all RAW hazards; forwarding fixes many cases but cannot change when the load's data physically arrives. The practical consequence is that we must either insert a one-cycle stall or schedule independent instructions into the gap. As you learn this material, remember that the load-use hazard is about timing — not correctness of the instruction semantics — and the stall preserves correct program behavior. How would you spot this pattern in an instruction stream?

Let's step through the five-stage pipeline cycles to see exactly when the load's data is produced and why the dependent instruction misses it. Assume a load instruction moves through IF, ID, EX, MEM, and WB across consecutive cycles. The data read from memory becomes available at the end of the MEM stage, and the register file write happens during WB. A dependent instruction that follows immediately will be in EX one cycle earlier — it needs the register operand at the beginning of its EX stage. Walking the cycles shows the mismatch: when LW is in MEM at cycle four, its dependent has already completed EX at cycle three and therefore cannot receive the loaded data in time. A one-cycle stall forces the dependent instruction to delay its EX stage until the load's data is available in the MEM/WB boundary so forwarding can supply it. A common misreading is to think writeback timing alone is the issue; the critical point is that forwarding can only forward data when it is present, and the load's data simply arrives too late for an immediately following EX. Given this timing, the simplest correct hardware response is a one-cycle stall that inserts a bubble into EX, letting MEM complete and data be forwarded to the delayed instruction.

Forwarding is excellent at resolving many read-after-write hazards because it takes a value as soon as it exists in later pipeline stages and supplies it to an earlier dependent stage. However, forwarding cannot conjure data before it has been produced. With a load instruction the data is only produced when the memory read completes, at the end of the MEM stage. If the dependent instruction's EX stage happens earlier, there is simply no value in a later stage to forward. Contrast this with a case where the previous instruction is an ALU operation: the result is available at the end of EX and can be forwarded into the next EX stage in time. A common misconception is to equate all RAW hazards with a forwarding solution; this is incorrect because the source of data matters. In short, a register written by an ALU instruction can be forwarded because the result exists earlier; a register written by a load does not. This timing contrast is the precise reason load-use hazards require special treatment — either a stall or rearrangement of instructions to delay the use.

When hazard detection logic recognizes a load-use pattern it executes a small, precise sequence of control actions to preserve correct execution: first, it stalls the IF and ID stages so the program counter does not advance and the instruction in ID is held in place. Second, it inserts a bubble — effectively a NOP — into the EX stage by preventing ID/EX from being updated; this bubble gives the load one cycle to move from EX into MEM so its data will be ready. The MEM and WB stages are allowed to proceed normally. The result is that the dependent instruction remains in ID for one extra cycle, then proceeds into EX when the data can be forwarded from MEM/WB. A pitfall when implementing stalls is forgetting to freeze the PC and IF stage, which would cause instruction fetch to continue and corrupt instruction ordering. Another subtle point is to ensure control signals to EX are neutralized for the inserted bubble. Correctly implemented, the stall is a single-cycle pause that preserves semantics while keeping hardware complexity low. Stall implementation mechanics means on detection: freeze if/id and pc, insert a nop into ex, and let mem/wb proceed so forwarding supplies the load's value on the next cycle.. In practical terms, exactly what the hazard unit does on detection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The hazard detection condition is concise and maps directly to pipeline registers. In practice we test whether the instruction in ID/EX is a load (MemRead set) and whether its destination register equals either source register of the instruction in IF/ID. Formally: ID/EX. MemRead AND (ID/EX. Rd == IF/ID. Rs1 OR ID/EX. Rd == IF/ID. Rs2). When this condition is true the hardware must stall. This check must use the proper pipeline-stage register fields and carefully compare register numbers, including zero checks if the ISA uses a zero register. A common mistake is to compare the wrong pipeline registers or to check for MemWrite instead of MemRead. Another subtlety is ensuring the comparison happens early enough in the cycle so stall control can freeze IF and ID before they update. The detection logic is intentionally simple: it prevents incorrect data use with a single boolean and small control path, which is why it is widely used in textbook five-stage pipelines. Hazard detection logic means trigger a stall when the id/ex stage is a load and its destination matches a source of the following instruction: id/ex.memread and (id/ex.rd == if/id.rs1 or id/ex.rd == if/id.rs2).. In practical terms, the boolean condition that triggers a load-use stall. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

We can quantify the performance effect of one-cycle load-use stalls with a simple formula: CPI equals the base CPI plus p times one extra cycle, where p is the frequency of load-use events. That is: CPI = CPI_base + p × 1. The chapter provides a numeric example to make this concrete. If 20% of instructions are loads and half of those loads are immediately followed by a dependent use, then p = 0.20 × 0.50 = 0.10. If CPI_base is 1.0, the new CPI becomes 1.10 — a measurable 10% slowdown. In pointer-chasing workloads nearly every load is followed by a use, so p approaches the load frequency and the CPI hit can be large. A common mistake is to apply the formula using the fraction of loads alone; instead, p must reflect the fraction of all instructions that are load-use pairs. Understanding this calculation helps you decide whether to optimize with compiler scheduling, loop unrolling, or to accept hardware complexity for out-of-order execution. As you profile a program, estimate load frequency and dependent rate to compute p and the expected CPI increase.

Pointer-chasing code — such as linked-list traversal or some tree traversals — often causes a very high rate of load-use pairs because each step loads a pointer and the next instruction immediately uses that pointer to compute the next address. In such code, almost every load is followed by a use, so the probability p approaches the load frequency itself. For example, if 25% of instructions are loads and almost every load is immediately used to compute the next memory address, p will be close to 0.25, producing a sizable CPI increase. The reason this pattern is harmful is that there are few independent instructions available to schedule into the delay slot; the program's data dependence chain prevents reordering without changing correctness. A common mistaken hope is that simple compiler scheduling will always eliminate stalls; pointer-chasing shows the limitation because there are no independent instructions to move. In these cases, hardware techniques such as out-of-order execution, load buffering, or value prediction are often necessary to regain performance. When analyzing applications, identify pointer-heavy kernels and measure p to decide whether software or hardware investment is warranted.

Compiler scheduling, also known as code motion or pipeline scheduling, reorders instructions so that independent operations occur between a load and its use. The goal is to fill the one-cycle delay slot and avoid the hardware stall. For example, consider three instructions: a load, an add that uses the load, and a later independent subtract. A simple scheduler can move the subtract between the load and the add, yielding no stall because the add's EX is delayed until the data arrives. A concrete before-and-after illustration: before scheduling: LW R1, 0(R2); ADD R3, R1, R4; SUB R5, R6, R7. After scheduling: LW R1, 0(R2); SUB R5, R6, R7; ADD R3, R1, R4. This transformation preserves program semantics when the moved instruction is truly independent. Now let's apply a scheduling pass to three example sequences to see how many load-use stalls can be eliminated. Sequence A is LW, ADD dependent on the load, then an independent SUB and an independent AND. The scheduler can place one of those independent instructions between the load and ADD, removing the single one-cycle stall. Sequence B has LW, ADD dependent on the load, then SUB that reads the load destination—this SUB depends on the same load, so it cannot be moved; the scheduler cannot eliminate the stall. Sequence C is a loop body with two loads and two dependent adds; with care the scheduler may interleave instructions if the loads are independent, but often there are limits. The hands-on activity described in the chapter asks you to write a pass that searches for load-use pairs, looks ahead for movable instructions, and reorders them. When no instruction can be moved, the pass should insert a NOP or leave the stall. This exercise highlights the limitations of scheduling: without independent instructions available you cannot remove the stall without unrolling or changing algorithms.

Loop unrolling duplicates the loop body multiple times to produce more independent instructions inside the expanded body. This creates additional candidates that the scheduler can move into delay slots between a load and its use. For example, a loop whose body is a single load and dependent add offers no scheduling room. After unrolling twice the body contains two loads and two adds; the compiler can then interleave load2 and add1 to hide the delay. The benefit is reduced stalls and lower branch overhead, often improving CPI substantially. The trade-offs are increased code size and higher register pressure, which may spill and offset the gains. Also, aggressive unrolling may expose additional opportunities for instruction-level parallelism, but requires careful register allocation and sometimes profile-guided heuristics. A common misconception is that unrolling always helps; in register-limited code the added pressure can make performance worse. Use unrolling selectively on hot loops where profiling shows high p and available registers to hold temporaries. When compiler techniques cannot remove load-use stalls because dependencies are inherent, hardware can help. Speculative load execution in out-of-order processors allows loads to be issued earlier than program order, overlapping memory access with other work and often reducing the perceived delay. Load buffering lets the processor make load data available from a buffer before it is written back to the register file, enabling dependent instructions to read from the buffer when safe. Value prediction attempts to guess the loaded value and execute dependent instructions speculatively; if the prediction is correct the stall is avoided, but on misprediction the dependent must be replayed. Each technique reduces stalls at increasing hardware complexity and risk. A common misconception is that hardware always beats software; in many cases a combined approach is best. For pointer-chasing or deep dependent chains hardware methods can provide material benefits, but they add verification, complexity, and potential replays that must be managed carefully. Summarizing the essentials: load-use hazards arise because loads produce data at the end of MEM while uses need it at the start of EX, creating a timing gap forwarding cannot bridge. The hardware fix is a one-cycle stall that freezes IF/ID and inserts a bubble into EX; the detection logic is ID/EX. MemRead AND register equality to IF/ID sources. The CPI impact is measured by CPI = CPI_base + p × 1, where p is the frequency of load-use pairs. Compiler scheduling and loop unrolling are effective software strategies when independent instructions are available; when they are not, hardware techniques like speculative loads, load buffering, or value prediction may be required. Pointer-chasing code often pushes p high and limits compiler options. Keep these compact rules in mind when optimizing: detect load-use patterns, quantify p, try scheduling and selective unrolling, and only add hardware complexity when software cannot solve the problem.

Keep three concise rules in mind. First, recognize the load-use timing gap: the load's value arrives at end of MEM while the dependent wants it at start of EX. Second, use the simple hardware response: detect the pattern, stall IF/ID, and insert a bubble into EX so forwarding can supply the value in the following cycle. Third, prefer compiler scheduling and loop unrolling when independent instructions exist; otherwise consider hardware approaches like speculative loads, load buffering, or value prediction. These three rules will let you analyze a workload, compute the CPI cost using p, and choose an appropriate mitigation strategy based on available code structure and acceptable hardware complexity.
